shuidiaogetou.summary: A two-part long song lyric (ci) to the tune Shuidiao getou. Su Shi looks at the moon on the Mid-Autumn night and misses his brother Su Zhe. He moves from questioning Heaven to imagining flying up there, then back to the human world, and finally eases the pain of parting with the lines 'I only wish that we may live long, and share the moon's beauty, a thousand li apart'. It is open-hearted and deeply felt.
shuidiaogetou.translation:
When did the bright moon first appear?
I raise my cup and ask the blue sky.
I do not know, in the palaces of the heavens,
what year it is tonight.
I would ride the wind and go back there,
but I fear the jade towers and crystal halls
are too cold to bear, so high up.
I rise and dance, playing with my clear shadow -
how can that compare with the human world?
She turns round the red pavilion, stoops to the carved windows,
and shines on those who cannot sleep.
She should have no grievance,
so why is she always full when people part?
People have sorrow and joy, parting and meeting;
the moon has dim and bright, full and waning:
from of old, nothing is ever whole.
I only wish that we may live long,
and share the moon's beauty, a thousand li apart.

glossary.note: The ninth year of Xining under Emperor Shenzong of the Song (1076).

glossary.en: qiong lou yu yu - jade towers and crystal halls
glossary.note: Splendid palaces built of fine jade; the palace of the moon.

glossary.en: bu ying you hen - she should have no grievance
glossary.note: The moon should have no reason for resentment; the poet is complaining that the moon is always full just when people part.
Of fine and lovely bearing; here, the moon.

shuidiaogetou.background: Su Shi (Su Dongpo) wrote this on the Mid-Autumn night of 1076 in Mizhou (today's Zhucheng in Shandong). The poem has a short preface saying that he wrote it after drinking, thinking of his younger brother Su Zhe (Ziyou).

niannujiao_chibi.summary: A long song lyric (ci) to the tune Niannujiao. Su Shi climbs to the Red Cliff, and from the grand scenery thinks of the heroic bearing and deeds of Zhou Yu of the Three Kingdoms. He contrasts that with his own age and unfinished career, and ends with 'Life is like a dream - let me pour one cup back to the river moon', where bold feeling mixes with detachment and sadness.
niannujiao_chibi.translation:
The great river flows east,
its waves washing away all the heroes of a thousand ages.
West of the old fortress, people say,
is the Red Cliff of Zhou Lang of the Three Kingdoms.
Jagged rocks pierce the sky, startling waves beat the shore,
rolling up a thousand heaps of snow.
Rivers and hills like a painting -
how many heroes there were in one age!
I think of Gongjin in those years:
Xiao Qiao had just become his bride,
and his bearing was bold and radiant.
With a feather fan and silk headband, laughing and talking,
the enemy's masts and oars flew off as ash and smoke.
My mind roams the old country;
the tender-hearted would laugh at me
for having grey hair so soon.
Life is like a dream -
let me pour one cup back to the river moon.

glossary.note: To scour or wash.
Zhou Yu, a famous general of Wu in the Three Kingdoms, who commanded at the Battle of Red Cliff.

glossary.en: yu shan guan jin - feather fan and silk headband
glossary.note: Holding a fan of feathers and wearing a headband of green silk; the look of a scholar-general.
Qiang is a mast and lu an oar (a variant writing of the same word): ships.
To pour wine on the ground as an offering. Read lei.

niannujiao_chibi.background: Su Shi wrote this in 1082 while exiled to Huangzhou. The 'Red Cliff' he visited was in fact the Red Nose Rock at Huangzhou, not the real site of the battle, and Su Shi kept his doubt in the words 'people say'. This lyric opened the bold and unrestrained style of ci.

jiangchengzi.summary: A two-part song lyric (ci) to the tune Jiangchengzi. Su Shi dreams of his dead wife: ten years of separation by death, a meeting in the dream where they face each other without a word and tears fall in a thousand lines. It ends by imagining her grave on a moonlit night under short pines, and is a famous elegy for a dead spouse.
jiangchengzi.translation:
Ten years, living and dead, both vast and blurred;
I do not try to think of you, yet cannot forget.
A lonely grave a thousand li away -
nowhere to tell of my desolation.
Even if we met, you would not know me:
dust over my face, my temples like frost.
Last night in a deep dream I suddenly went home;
by the small window of the little room, you were at your dressing.
We looked at each other without a word,
and only tears ran in a thousand lines.
I know the place that breaks my heart year after year:
a moonlit night, on a hill of short pines.

glossary.note: The eighth year of Xining under Emperor Shenzong of the Song (1075).

glossary.en: qian li gu fen - a lonely grave a thousand li away
glossary.note: His wife Wang Fu was buried at Meishan in Sichuan, a thousand li from Mizhou where he was.

glossary.en: xuan chuang - a room with a window
glossary.note: A small room with a window.

glossary.en: duan song gang - a hill of short pines
glossary.note: A hill planted with small pine trees; a grave.

jiangchengzi.background: The poem's title reads 'Recording a dream on the night of the twentieth of the first month, Yimao'. In 1075, in Mizhou, Su Shi dreamed of his wife Wang Fu, who had died ten years earlier, and wrote this.

dingfengbo.summary: A two-part song lyric (ci) to the tune Dingfengbo. Su Shi is caught in rain on the road while his companions are in a sorry state, but he walks slowly and chants calmly. With a bamboo staff, straw sandals and a straw cloak in mist and rain, he shows no fear of storms, and ends with 'no wind and rain, and no clearing either', a mind free and open.
dingfengbo.translation:
Do not listen to the rain beating through the woods and on the leaves;
why not chant and whistle and walk slowly?
A bamboo staff and straw sandals are lighter than a horse -
who is afraid?
A straw cloak in mist and rain, for all my life.
The sharp spring wind blows me sober;
a little cold,
but the slanting sun on the hilltop comes to greet me.
Looking back at the place of bleak wind and rain,
I go home:
no wind and rain, and no clearing either.

glossary.en: chuan lin da ye - beating through the woods and on the leaves
glossary.note: Rain falling through the trees and striking the leaves.
Sandals made of straw.
Describes the chill of early spring.

glossary.en: xiao se chu - the place of bleak wind and rain
glossary.note: A place where wind and rain beat the trees.

dingfengbo.background: A short preface says that on the seventh day of the third month, on the road to Sha Lake, they met rain; the rain gear had gone ahead, and everyone in the party was in a sorry state except Su Shi, who did not notice, and soon it cleared, so he wrote this. It dates from 1082, while he was exiled to Huangzhou.

busuanzi_su.summary: A short two-part song lyric (ci) to the tune Busuanzi. Su Shi uses a lone wild goose as a picture of himself: a waning moon, sparse parasol trees, the still of deep night, and the goose that starts up and looks back. It expresses a proud loneliness in exile that will not follow the common way.
busuanzi_su.translation:
A waning moon hangs on the sparse parasol trees;
the water-clock has stopped and people are just quiet.
Who sees the lone recluse come and go,
like the faint shadow of a lonely wild goose?
Startled, it rises and looks back,
with a grief no one understands.
It picks over every cold branch and will not perch,
and lodges on the lonely cold sandbar.

glossary.en: lou duan - the water-clock has stopped
glossary.note: The lou is the old water-clock; when it has stopped, the night is deep.
One who lives in retirement; the poet himself.
Dim and indistinct.
To comprehend. Read xing.

busuanzi_su.background: Su Shi wrote this during his exile in Huangzhou (about 1080-1081). The poem's title is 'Written While Lodging at the Dinghui Temple in Huangzhou'.

shengshengman.summary: A two-part long song lyric (ci) to the tune Shengshengman. Li Qingzhao opens with fourteen repeated characters to describe the desolation of living alone after the fall of her country and the death of her husband. The wild goose, the yellow flowers, the parasol trees and the fine rain all stir her sorrow, and the last line 'how can a single word, sorrow, cover it?' says that the grief is too heavy to put into words.
shengshengman.translation:
Searching, seeking,
cold, bleak,
miserable, sorrowful and sad.
In the time of sudden warmth and returning cold,
it is hardest to take rest.
How can three or two cups of thin wine
stand against the wind rising in the evening?
The wild geese pass over,
just when I am heartbroken -
they are old acquaintances.
The ground is heaped with yellow flowers,
withered and spoiled; now who would pick them?
Keeping by the window,
how can I get through to dark alone?
The parasol trees, and fine rain besides,
drip and drop till dusk.
At a time like this,
how can a single word, 'sorrow', cover it!

glossary.en: zha nuan huan han - suddenly warm, then cold again
glossary.note: Sudden warmth followed by cold.

glossary.en: jiang xi - to rest and recover
glossary.note: To rest, look after oneself.
Chrysanthemums.
The situation, the circumstances.
How, in what way.

shengshengman.background: Li Qingzhao wrote this in her later years, after the court fled south. Her husband Zhao Mingcheng had died, and she was drifting alone. The opening in repeated characters is the greatest feature of this lyric.

zuihuayin.summary: A two-part short song lyric (ci) to the tune Zuihuayin. On the Double Ninth festival Li Qingzhao thinks of her far-away husband. She draws thin mist and thick cloud, the incense burned out in its golden beast, and drinking at the eastern hedge in loneliness, and ends with the famous line 'the person is thinner than the yellow flowers', showing the pain of longing.
zuihuayin.translation:
Thin mist and thick cloud, sorrow through the long day;
the camphor burns out in the golden beast.
Another festival day, the Double Ninth -
on the jade pillow, within the gauze curtain,
the chill of midnight has just come through.
After dusk I drink at the eastern hedge,
and a hidden fragrance fills my sleeves.
Do not say it does not melt the soul!
The curtain is rolled up by the west wind,
and the person is thinner than the yellow flowers.

glossary.note: A long daytime.
A fragrance, borneol (dragon-brain) incense.
A bronze incense burner in the shape of an animal.
A mosquito-net bed hanging of gauze.

glossary.en: xiao hun - to melt the soul
glossary.note: Describes the extreme of sorrow or of joy.

zuihuayin.background: This is an early work by Li Qingzhao, a poem of longing sent to her husband Zhao Mingcheng. The story goes that when Zhao Mingcheng read it he felt he could not match it, shut himself away to think hard, and still could not surpass it.

rumengling.summary: A one-part short song lyric (ci) to the tune Rumengling. Li Qingzhao recalls the evening when, as a young girl, she was drinking at a stream pavilion and lost her way home by boat, drifting deep into the lotus and startling gulls and herons. The language is bright and quick, full of the spirit of youth.
rumengling.translation:
I often remember an evening at the stream pavilion,
drunk and unaware of the way home.
When the fun was done I turned the boat late,
and strayed into the depths of the lotus.
How do we get out? How do we get out?
Up flew a whole shoal of gulls and herons.

glossary.note: A pavilion on the bank of a stream.
Evening.
Lotus blossoms.

glossary.en: zheng du - how to get across
glossary.note: Zheng here means 'how'; the line asks how to row through.

rumengling.background: Li Qingzhao wrote this in her early years in Jinan. The style is fresh and lively, very different from the sorrowful style of her later years.

yijianmei.summary: A two-part song lyric (ci) to the tune Yijianmei. Li Qingzhao writes of longing after parting from her husband: the withered lotus, the chill bamboo mat of autumn, going alone onto the orchid boat, the lines of wild geese and the moon full over the west tower. It ends with 'just gone from the brows, it climbs into the heart', for a sorrow that cannot be got rid of.
yijianmei.translation:
The red lotus has lost its scent, the jade mat is cold with autumn.
I loosen my gauze skirt lightly
and step alone onto the orchid boat.
Who sends a brocade letter from beyond the clouds?
When the wild geese return in their lines,
the moon is full over the west tower.
Flowers drift and fall by themselves, the water flows by itself;
one kind of longing, in two places, an idle sorrow.
There is no way to put this feeling away:
just gone from the brows,
it climbs into the heart.

glossary.en: yu dian - a fine bamboo mat
glossary.note: A beautiful bamboo sleeping mat. Dian is read dian.
A letter. The phrase comes from Su Hui, who wove a palindrome poem in brocade and sent it to her husband.

glossary.en: yan zi - characters of wild geese
glossary.note: Wild geese in flight form a line like the character for 'one' or 'person'.
A sorrow with no clear cause.

yijianmei.background: Not long after Li Qingzhao's marriage, Zhao Mingcheng went away to study, and she wrote this to express her feelings. Lines such as 'flowers drift and fall by themselves, the water flows by itself' are among her most famous.

yulinling.summary: A two-part long song lyric (ci) to the tune Yulinling. Liu Yong writes of parting from his lover: the sudden rain at the long pavilion, the orchid boat urging departure, hands held in silence. He then imagines the dawn wind and waning moon when the wine wears off after parting. It is one of the great Song poems of parting.
yulinling.translation:
Cold cicadas sing, shrill and sad;
I face the long pavilion at evening, the sudden rain just stopped.
Drinking in a tent at the city gate, I have no heart for it;
just as I linger, the orchid boat urges departure.
Hand in hand we look at each other, eyes full of tears,
and in the end no words come, only a choking throat.
I think of going, going, a thousand li of misty waves,
evening mist heavy, the Chu sky wide.
Tender hearts have always been hurt by parting,
and how much worse in the bleak season of clear autumn!
Where shall I be tonight when the wine wears off?
On a willow bank, in morning wind and a waning moon.
This journey will last years;
the good days and fine scenes will be set out for nothing.
Even if I had a thousand kinds of feeling,
to whom could I tell them?

glossary.note: A roadside pavilion of the old days where travellers rested and farewells were held.

glossary.en: du men zhang yin - a farewell drink in a tent outside the capital gate
glossary.note: A tent set up outside the capital for a parting feast.
A boat of magnolia wood; a pleasing name for a boat.
The throat closes so that no words come.

glossary.en: xiao feng can yue - morning wind and waning moon
glossary.note: The wind just before dawn and the moon about to set.

yulinling.background: Liu Yong was a Northern Song poet of the 'delicate and restrained' (wanyue) school who excelled at the long form of ci. This lyric describes a parting from a lover in Bianjing (the capital) and is his best-known work.

bashengganzhou.summary: A two-part long song lyric (ci) to the tune Bashengganzhou. Liu Yong paints an autumn dusk on his travels - evening rain over river and sky, frosty wind, passes and rivers - and climbs high with thoughts of home. He then imagines his lover waiting at home, so that distance and longing weigh on both sides.
bashengganzhou.translation:
Facing the pouring evening rain that sprays over the river sky,
it has washed the clear autumn once over.
Slowly the frosty wind turns bleak and sharp,
the passes and rivers are cold and empty,
and the last light rests on the tower.
Everywhere the red fades and the green wanes;
little by little the beauty of things is finished.
Only the waters of the Yangtze
flow east without a word.
I cannot bear to climb high and look far,
to gaze at my far-off home,
my longing to return hard to rein in.
I sigh at my travels these years -
why do I stay so long in pain?
I think of my lovely one in her dressing tower, craning her neck:
how many times has she mistaken
a boat at the edge of the sky for my homecoming?
How could she know that I, leaning on the railing,
am just as lost in sorrow?

glossary.note: The name of the tune, originally a Tang frontier song.
Mountain passes and rivers.
The fine sights of the season.
To lift the head and gaze. Read yong.
So, in this way.

bashengganzhou.background: This is the best-known example of Liu Yong's travel poems. It is said that Su Shi once praised the three lines 'Slowly the frosty wind turns bleak and sharp, the passes and rivers are cold and empty, and the last light rests on the tower', saying that even the Tang poets at their best did no better.

dielianhua_liu.summary: A two-part song lyric (ci) to the tune Dielianhua. Liu Yong climbs a high place and looks into the distance, with a spring sorrow that has no cause. He tries to drown it in wine, but forced cheer is tasteless. He ends with 'My belt grows looser and I never regret it; for her, I am glad to grow haggard', a loyalty that does not regret wasting away for love.
dielianhua_liu.translation:
I stand long leaning on the high tower, the wind soft and thin;
gazing as far as I can, a spring sorrow
rises dark from the edge of the sky.
The colour of grass, the haze of light, in the last sun -
no one speaks; who will understand why I lean on the rail?
I thought to give way to wildness and get drunk,
to sing to the wine,
but forced cheer has no taste.
My belt grows looser and I never regret it:
for her, I am glad to grow haggard.

glossary.en: zhu yi - to stand and lean
glossary.note: To stand a long time leaning on something.
A tall building.
Dark and gloomy.
Free of restraint, unruly.
A pronoun for 'she'.

dielianhua_liu.background: By Liu Yong. Wang Guowei quoted the last two lines as the second stage of those who 'succeed in great enterprises and great learning, from ancient times to now'. One tradition says the lyric is by Ouyang Xiu.

manjianghong.summary: A two-part long song lyric (ci) to the tune Manjianghong. Yue Fei sets out his resolve to recover the Central Plains, his anger at the shame of Jingkang, and his vow to kill the enemy and win merit and restore the land. It is bold and grand, full of patriotic fire.
manjianghong.translation:
Hair on end with rage, lifting my cap,
I lean on the rail as the whistling rain stops.
I raise my eyes and, facing the sky, give a long cry;
my fierce heart burns high.
Thirty years of fame and merit are dust and earth;
eight thousand li of road under cloud and moon.
Do not idly let the young head turn white
and grieve in vain.
The shame of Jingkang is not yet washed away;
the vassal's regret - when will it be gone?
I will drive long chariots and trample down
the gap in Helan Mountain.
With high resolve, I eat the flesh of the barbarian foe when hungry;
laughing and talking, I drink the blood of the Xiongnu when thirsty.
Let me start again from the beginning,
gather up the old rivers and mountains,
and present myself at the heavenly gate.

glossary.en: ping lan - to lean on the rail
glossary.note: To lean on a railing.

glossary.en: Jingkang chi - the shame of Jingkang
glossary.note: In the second year of Jingkang (1127), the Jin army broke into Bianjing and carried off the two emperors, Huizong and Qinzong.
On the border of today's Ningxia and Inner Mongolia; here it stands for the Jin frontier.
The imperial palace, the court.

manjianghong.background: This lyric is traditionally ascribed to Yue Fei, but scholars dispute who wrote it and when. 'The shame of Jingkang' in the poem means the shame of the fall of the Northern Song.

qingyuan_xi.summary: A two-part song lyric (ci) to the tune Qingyuan'an. Xin Qiji describes the lantern night of the first full moon: flower lanterns, fireworks, perfumed carriages and the fish and dragon lanterns dancing. But the one he looks for in the crowd stands alone where the lamplight is thin, which carries the poet's own lofty solitude that will not follow the crowd.
qingyuan_xi.translation:
The east wind opens a thousand trees of flowers in the night,
and blows down stars like rain.
Precious horses and carved carriages leave fragrance all along the road;
phoenix flutes sound, the jade jar of the moon turns its light,
and all night the fish and dragon lanterns dance.
Moth ornaments, snow willows, golden threads,
laughing voices full of charm pass by with a hidden fragrance.
I search for her in the crowd a thousand, a hundred times;
then suddenly I turn my head -
and there she is, where the lamplight is thin.

glossary.en: yuan xi - the night of the Lantern Festival
glossary.note: The night of the fifteenth of the first lunar month, the Lantern Festival.

glossary.en: xing ru yu - stars like rain
glossary.note: Fireworks falling like a shower of shooting stars.
The moon; another reading takes it as a lantern made of jade.

glossary.en: yu long wu - fish and dragon dancing
glossary.note: Lanterns shaped like fish and dragons being waved in the dance.
Sparse, nearly out.

qingyuan_xi.background: By Xin Qiji. In his Remarks on Lyrics in the Human World (Renjian cihua), Wang Guowei took the line 'then suddenly I turn my head, and there she is, where the lamplight is thin' as an image of the third stage of success in scholarship.

pozhenzi.summary: A two-part song lyric (ci) to the tune Pozhenzi. Xin Qiji recalls his army years as a young man: looking at his sword by lamplight in drink, dreaming of the camps, reviewing troops on the field. The last line, 'alas, white hair has grown', laments that his high purpose is unfulfilled and his hair has turned white.

glossary.note: Chen Liang, courtesy name Tongfu, a friend of Xin Qiji who also argued for war with the north.
Under one's command, one's men.
Meat roasted over a fire.
The ancient zither (se) had fifty strings; here it means all kinds of instruments.
The name of a fast horse ridden by Liu Bei.

pozhenzi.background: The title is 'Written in Bold Words for Chen Tongfu, and Sent to Him'. Xin Qiji wrote it while living in retirement in Jiangxi, and sent it to Chen Liang, who shared his aims.

yongyule.summary: A two-part long song lyric (ci) to the tune Yongyule. Xin Qiji climbs the Beigu Pavilion at Jingkou and remembers heroes such as Sun Quan and Liu Yu. He criticises the Southern Song rulers for a hasty northern campaign and for being content with a corner of the land, and he compares himself to Lian Po, old and unemployed.
yongyule.translation:
The rivers and hills of a thousand ages:
nowhere to find a hero like Sun Zhongmou.
Dancing halls and singing terraces,
all that grace and glamour swept away by wind and rain.
Grass and trees in the slanting sun,
an ordinary lane - people say
Jinu once lived there.
I think of those years: golden spears and iron horses,
a spirit swallowing ten thousand li like a tiger.
In Yuanjia, in haste,
they sealed the hill at Wolf-Dwelling and won only a panicked look north.
Forty-three years:
in my sight I still remember
the lamplit road to Yangzhou.
How can I bear to look back?
Beneath the Temple of Foli,
a crowd of sacred crows and village drums.
Whom can I ask:
Lian Po is old - can he still eat his rice?

glossary.note: Today's Zhenjiang in Jiangsu.
Sun Quan, courtesy name Zhongmou, who made Jingkou his capital.
The childhood name of Liu Yu, founder of the Liu Song dynasty (420-479) of the Southern Dynasties, a native of Jingkou.
The Han general Huo Qubing chased the Xiongnu to Wolf-Dwelling Hill and made an altar to Heaven there; it stands for a great victory.

glossary.en: Foli ci - the Temple of Foli
glossary.note: A palace built during the southern invasion of Emperor Taiwu of the Northern Wei (whose childhood name was Foli), later turned into a temple.

glossary.en: Lian Po lao yi - Lian Po is old
glossary.note: Lian Po was set aside by the king of Zhao yet in old age could still eat well; the poet uses it of himself.

yongyule.background: Xin Qiji wrote this in 1205, when he was prefect of Zhenjiang at the age of sixty-six. Forty-three years had passed since he came south at twenty-two.

moyuer.summary: A two-part long song lyric (ci) to the tune Moyuer. Xin Qiji uses cherishing, resenting and trying to keep spring as a cover for his worries and disappointments in politics. The end warns those in favour not to be too proud, and 'the slanting sun is there, over the misty willows, a place of heartbreak' leaves a long lingering feeling.
moyuer.translation:
How many more storms of wind and rain can it take?
In haste, spring is going again.
I cherish spring, always afraid the flowers open too early -
how much more now, with fallen red beyond counting!
Spring, stay a while!
I hear that at the edge of the sky the fragrant grass leaves no road home.
I resent spring for saying nothing;
only, it seems, the spider webs on the painted eaves are attentive,
catching drifting catkins all day long.
The matter of Changmen:
a happy meeting promised was missed again,
and once there was someone who envied the moth-eyebrows.
Though a thousand gold could buy Xiangru's rhapsody,
to whom can this unspoken feeling be told?
Do not dance, my lord!
Do you not see how Yuhuan and Feiyan have all turned to dust?
Idle sorrow is the bitterest.
Do not go and lean on the high rail:
the slanting sun is there
over the misty willows, a place of heartbreak.

glossary.note: To bear.

glossary.en: Changmen shi - the matter of Changmen
glossary.note: Empress Chen Ajiao of Emperor Wu of Han fell out of favour and was sent to the Changmen Palace.
Sima Xiangru wrote the 'Rhapsody of Changmen' to plead the Empress's case to the emperor.

glossary.en: Yuhuan Feiyan - Yang Yuhuan and Zhao Feiyan
glossary.note: Both were loved by their emperors and both met a bad end.
A railing in a high place.

moyuer.background: Xin Qiji wrote this in 1179 when he was transferred from Hubei to Hunan as vice commissioner for transport. The fleeting spring carries his worry about the state.

pusaman_xin.summary: A two-part short song lyric (ci) to the tune Pusaman. Xin Qiji climbs Yugu Terrace and sees the Gan River rushing along, and remembers how the Jin army once chased Empress Dowager Longyou. The hills cannot hold back the river, as they cannot hide the grief for the lost northern lands, and the partridge's cry at the end deepens his sorrow.
pusaman_xin.translation:
Below Yugu Terrace flows the clear river,
and in between, how many travellers' tears.
To the north-west is Chang'an,
and alas, countless hills in between.
Green hills cannot hold it back;
after all the river flows on.
At evening on the river, just as I grieve,
deep in the hills I hear the partridge.

glossary.note: In today's Ganzhou in Jiangxi, above the Gan River.
The upper reaches of the Gan River.
In today's Wan'an county in Jiangxi, where Empress Dowager Longyou was chased by the Jin army in the early Southern Song.
A bird whose call sounds to Chinese ears like 'you cannot go, elder brother'.

pusaman_xin.background: Xin Qiji wrote this on the wall at Zaokou when he passed through as Jiangxi's criminal justice commissioner (around the third or fourth year of Chunxi).

yumeiren.summary: A two-part short song lyric (ci) to the tune Yumeiren. Li Yu, imprisoned after the fall of his state, remembers spring flowers, the autumn moon and the old country, and contrasts then and now. The question 'how much sorrow do you have?' is answered with 'like a river of spring water flowing east', a line known for a thousand years, said to be his last lyric.
yumeiren.translation:
When will spring flowers and autumn moon be done?
How much of the past do I know?
Last night the east wind came again to the small tower -
I cannot bear to look back on my old country in the bright moonlight.
The carved rails and jade steps must still be there,
only the rosy faces have changed.
If you ask how much sorrow I have,
it is like a river of spring water flowing east.

glossary.note: To finish, to come to an end.
Here, the Southern Tang.

glossary.en: diao lan yu qi - carved rails and jade steps
glossary.note: Carved railings and jade-stone steps; the palace.

glossary.en: zhu yan gai - rosy faces changed
glossary.note: Faces have aged; it also means that people and times have changed.

yumeiren.background: Li Yu was the last ruler of the Southern Tang. After his state fell he was taken to Bianjing and given the title of Marquis Who Defied His Orders. The story is that Emperor Taizong of the Song heard of this lyric and sent him poisoned wine.

xianghuan.summary: A two-part short song lyric (ci) to the tune Xianghuan. Imprisoned, Li Yu climbs the west tower alone: a hooked moon, lonely parasol trees, a courtyard that locks up the clear autumn. 'Cut, it will not break; sorted, it only tangles worse' is how he describes the grief of parting, and the last line says the strange taste of this sorrow cannot be named.
xianghuan.translation:
Without a word, alone I climb the west tower;
the moon is like a hook.
Lonely parasol trees, a deep courtyard locking in the clear autumn.
Cut, it will not break; sorted, it only tangles worse -
this is the grief of parting.
Another kind of taste sits in the heart.

glossary.note: The tower where he was held.

glossary.en: yue ru gou - the moon like a hook
glossary.note: A crescent moon like a hook.

glossary.en: suo qing qiu - locking in clear autumn
glossary.note: Autumn shut inside the deep courtyard.

glossary.en: li chou - the grief of parting
glossary.note: Sorrow at parting.

xianghuan.background: Li Yu wrote this when he was held in Bianjing after the fall of his state. Like 'Yumeiren', it is one of his best-known later works.

sumuzhe.summary: A two-part song lyric (ci) to the tune Sumuzhe. Fan Zhongyan paints an autumn scene on a grand scale - blue clouds, yellow leaves, setting sun, fragrant grass - which leads to homesickness. The second part describes sleepless nights and wine that turns into tears of longing for home.
sumuzhe.translation:
Blue clouds in the sky, yellow leaves on the ground;
autumn colour joins the waves, and on the waves cold mist is green.
The hills catch the slanting sun and the sky meets the water.
The fragrant grass, heartless,
lies still further beyond the setting sun.
My homesick soul is dimmed, and traveller's thoughts pursue me;
every night, unless a good dream
keeps me asleep.
When the bright moon lights the high tower, do not lean there alone:
wine enters the sorrowing gut
and turns to tears of longing.

glossary.en: an xiang hun - a dimmed homesick soul
glossary.note: The spirit darkened by thoughts of home.

glossary.en: zhui lv si - travel thoughts that pursue
glossary.note: The sorrow of a traveller follows close behind.

glossary.en: ye ye chu fei - every night, unless
glossary.note: Each night, only a good dream will let him sleep.
A heart full of sorrow.

sumuzhe.background: Fan Zhongyan was a famous minister of the Northern Song. He wrote this while guarding the north-western frontier, describing the autumn scenes of the border and his longing for home in a heavy, sombre style.

huanxisha.summary: A two-part short song lyric (ci) to the tune Huanxisha. Yan Shu listens to a new song and drinks beside a pond and terrace, sighing over passing time: flowers fall and nothing can be done, swallows return as if known, and he paces alone on the scented garden path. There is a light sadness and a thought about the way of things.

glossary.note: A newly written lyric.

glossary.en: qu nian tian qi jiu ting tai - last year's weather, the old pavilion
glossary.note: The same weather and the same terrace as last year.

glossary.en: wu ke nai he - nothing can be done
glossary.note: There is no way out.
A path full of the scent of flowers.

huanxisha.background: Yan Shu was a Northern Song poet of the delicate school who rose to be chief minister. The matching pair 'Flowers fall, and nothing can be done; swallows come back, as though I knew them' first appeared in one of his poems and was then used in this lyric, where it became a famous couplet.

dielianhua_ouyang.summary: A two-part song lyric (ci) to the tune Dielianhua. A wife in the inner rooms keeps an empty courtyard in late spring while her husband roams and does not come home. Layers of curtains, slanting rain and raging wind, and asking the flowers with tearful eyes show deep resentment, and the scattered red petals flying past the swing at the end add to the sadness.
dielianhua_ouyang.translation:
The courtyard is deep, deep, deep - how deep?
Willows pile up like mist,
and the curtains are past counting.
Jade-bridled horses, carved saddles, where he goes to play;
the tower is high and cannot see the Zhangtai road.
Rain slants and wind rages at the end of the third month;
the door is shut at dusk, and there is no way to keep spring.
With tearful eyes I ask the flowers; the flowers do not speak,
and scattered red blossoms fly past the swing.

glossary.en: yu le diao an - jade bridle, carved saddle
glossary.note: A bridle set with jade and a carved saddle; a rich horse and carriage.

glossary.en: you ye chu - a place of pleasure
glossary.note: A place for wandering and enjoyment.
A street in Chang'an in the Han dynasty (206 BC-220 AD), where singing girls lived.
Fallen petals tossed about.

dielianhua_ouyang.background: Who wrote this lyric has long been argued, with Ouyang Xiu and Feng Yanji both named; it is included in both Liuyi ci and Yangchun ji.

queqiaoxian.summary: A two-part short song lyric (ci) to the tune Queqiaoxian. Qin Guan writes of the meeting of the Cowherd and the Weaver Girl on the seventh night of the seventh month: their yearly meeting is better than countless meetings in the human world. The last lines, 'If two hearts are bound for a long time, why must they be together morning and evening?', give a new thought, that love does not depend on being together day and night.
queqiaoxian.translation:
Slender clouds play at clever shapes, shooting stars carry their grief,
and across the far Silver River they cross unseen.
Once they meet in the golden wind and jade dew,
it is better than countless meetings in the human world.
Tenderness like water, a happy meeting like a dream -
how can they bear to look back on the road over the magpie bridge?
If two hearts are bound for a long time,
why must they be together morning and evening?

glossary.en: nong qiao - to play at cleverness
glossary.note: To make clever patterns; the seventh night is also called the festival of begging for skill.
The Milky Way.

glossary.en: jin feng yu lu - golden wind and jade dew
glossary.note: Autumn wind and white dew; autumn.
The legend that on the seventh night magpies make a bridge for the Cowherd and Weaver Girl to meet.

queqiaoxian.background: Qin Guan was a Northern Song poet, one of the 'Four Scholars of Su's Circle', with a delicate style. This is a famous poem for the Qixi festival.

manTingfang.summary: A two-part long song lyric (ci) to the tune Manting fang. Qin Guan writes of parting from a singing girl: thin cloud brushing the hills, the sky sticking to the withered grass, slanting sun, cold crows, a stream round a lone village. He remembers old times, the sachet quietly loosened and the silk belt lightly parted, and at last strains to see the high city, where the lamps already show at dusk. It is full of grief and tenderness.
manTingfang.translation:
The hills are brushed with thin cloud, the sky sticks to the withered grass,
and the sound of the painted horn breaks off at the watchtower gate.
I halt my travelling oars for a while,
and lift this parting cup with you.
So many old affairs of Penglai -
I look back in vain at the swirling mist.
Beyond the slanting sun,
ten thousand specks of cold crows,
and flowing water winding round a lone village.
Soul-melting, at such a moment:
the scented sachet is quietly loosened, the silk belt lightly parted.
In vain I have won only a name in the green houses -
the name of a fickle man remains.
When shall we meet again after this journey?
On my sleeves, only the traces of tears.
At the place of sorrow, I strain my eyes at the high city,
where the lamps already show at dusk.

glossary.note: To smear or lightly sweep across.
The gate tower on a city wall.

glossary.en: yin li zun - to lift the parting cup
glossary.note: To raise a farewell cup.

glossary.en: Penglai jiu shi - old affairs of Penglai
glossary.note: The happy past with the singing girl.
Brothels, singing houses.
Heartless, unfaithful.

manTingfang.background: By Qin Guan. Because the opening line 'The hills are brushed with thin cloud' was so fine, Qin Guan was nicknamed 'Master Hills-Brushed-with-Cloud'.

guizhixiang.summary: A two-part long song lyric (ci) to the tune Guizhixiang. Wang Anshi climbs high at Jinling and describes the grandeur of the land in late autumn, then looks back at the rise and fall of the Six Dynasties and criticises those who only chase pleasure. It ends with the leftover tune 'Flowers in the Rear Courtyard' and carries a deep warning.
guizhixiang.translation:
Climbing up to gaze far,
it is just late autumn in the old capital, the air newly stern.
A thousand li of clear river like white silk,
green peaks gathered like clusters.
Returning sails and departing oars in the setting sun;
against the west wind, the tavern flag stands slanting.
Painted boats in thin cloud, egrets rising from the Milky Way -
a picture could hardly capture it.
I think of the past, of rivalry in splendour,
and sigh: outside the gate, atop the tower,
grief and regret followed one another.
Looking down from a height through a thousand years,
people idly sigh over glory and disgrace.
The old affairs of the Six Dynasties went with the flowing water;
only cold mist and fragrant grass stand green.
Even now the singing girls
still, from time to time, sing
the leftover tune of 'Flowers in the Rear Courtyard'.

glossary.note: Jinling, the old capital of the Six Dynasties.

glossary.en: cheng jiang si lian - the clear river like white silk
glossary.note: The clear river like a length of white silk.

glossary.en: men wai lou tou - outside the gate, atop the tower
glossary.note: From Du Mu's poem on Taicheng: 'Han Qinhu is outside the gate, Zhang Lihua atop the tower'. It means that when the Sui troops attacked Chen, the last Chen ruler was still enjoying himself in the palace.
Wu, Eastern Jin, Song, Qi, Liang and Chen, all with their capital at Jinling.
'Flowers of Jade Trees in the Rear Courtyard', written by the last ruler of Chen, a tune of a doomed state.

guizhixiang.background: Wang Anshi wrote this in his later years at Jinling (today's Nanjing). The lyric looks back on the past and also holds a criticism of the court of his day.

qingyuan_he.summary: A two-part song lyric (ci) to the tune Qingyuan'an. He Zhu writes of the sadness of watching a beautiful woman go and never seeing her again. The last three images, 'a plain of misty grass, a town full of willow down, the rain when plums are yellow', measure how much sorrow he has, and for this he was nicknamed 'He of the Plums'.
qingyuan_he.translation:
She does not cross, with her wave-treading step, the road to Hengtang;
I can only watch with my eyes as her fragrant dust goes.
With whom does she spend her brocade-zither youth?
The moon bridge, the flowered courtyard, the latticed window and red door -
only spring knows the place.
Flying clouds drift slowly over the evening marsh of fragrant grass;
with a coloured brush I write new heartbreaking lines.
If you ask how much idle sorrow there is:
a plain of misty grass,
a town full of willow down,
and the rain when plums are yellow.

glossary.note: Describes a woman's light step; the phrase comes from Cao Zhi's 'Rhapsody on the Goddess of the Luo'.
To the south-west of today's Suzhou.

glossary.en: jin se hua nian - brocade zither, flowering years
glossary.note: The beautiful years of youth.

glossary.en: heng gao - a bank of fragrant grass
glossary.note: A high bank by the water, grown with fragrant du heng plants.

glossary.en: mei zi huang shi yu - rain when plums turn yellow
glossary.note: The long drizzle of the plum-rain season in the Jiangnan region.

qingyuan_he.background: By He Zhu. Because the closing lines were so good, he was called 'He of the Plums'. He wrote this when he had retired to Hengtang in Suzhou.

yangzhoumanl.summary: A two-part long song lyric (ci) to the tune Yangzhou man. Jiang Kui passes through Yangzhou after the wars and finds the old famous city desolate. In the empty city, with the cold horn, he sighs that even Du Mu could not write such deep feeling; the Twenty-four Bridges still stand, a cold moon rocks silently on the water, and he asks for whom the red peonies bloom each year. It is a lament for a ruined homeland.
yangzhoumanl.translation:
A famous city east of the Huai, the fine place at Zhuxi:
I unsaddle and stop a little at the start of my journey.
Passing ten li of spring wind,
all is green with shepherd's purse and wheat.
Since the Tartar horses peered at the river and left,
the ruined pools and tall trees
still hate to speak of war.
Slowly dusk comes, the clear horn blows cold,
all in an empty city.
Master Du Mu, that keen admirer of fine sights -
I reckon that if he came again now he would be startled.
Though his cardamom poem was skilful
and his dream of the green houses sweet,
it would be hard for him to write this deep feeling.
The Twenty-four Bridges still stand;
a cold moon rocks silent in the heart of the waves.
I think of the red peonies by the bridge:
for whom do they know to bloom, year after year?

glossary.en: Huai zuo - east of the Huai
glossary.note: East of the Huai River; Yangzhou was once part of the eastern circuit of Huainan.
A pavilion that is a famous sight in Yangzhou.

glossary.en: Hu ma kui jiang - Tartar horses peering at the river
glossary.note: The Jin army's attacks on the south, which reached Yangzhou.
From Du Mu's 'Parting Gift': 'Slender and graceful, a little over thirteen, like a cardamom bud at the start of the second month'.
A famous bridge in Yangzhou; some say it means twenty-four bridges, others that it is the name of one bridge.

yangzhoumanl.background: At the winter solstice of 1176 Jiang Kui passed through Yangzhou, saw the desolation after the war, and composed this tune himself (a self-made tune, zidu qu). Jiang Kui was a Southern Song poet and a gifted musician, whose style is pure, spare and elegant.

tangduoling.summary: A two-part song lyric (ci) to the tune Tangduoling. Wu Wenying splits the character for 'sorrow' into 'autumn' above 'heart', saying that parting sorrow grows in the heart. He writes of plantain, cool wind and a bright moon he fears to climb a tower under; in the second part, flowers are gone, the swallows return, the guest lingers, and even drooping willows cannot tie a boat, leaving a helpless sadness.
tangduoling.translation:
Where is sorrow put together?
Autumn upon the heart of the parted one.
Even if the plantain gets no rain, it rustles all the same.
Everyone says the evening cool is fine weather,
and there is a bright moon,
but I fear to climb the tower.
The affairs of years end in dreams;
the flowers are gone and the misty water flows;
the swallows have taken leave and gone home, but the traveller still lingers.
The drooping willows do not wind round her skirt-sash to hold her;
they only, in vain, tie up the travelling boat.

glossary.note: To assemble. Here the poet splits a character: above the heart of a parting person is the character for sorrow (autumn plus heart).
Even if.

glossary.en: sou sou - the sound of wind
glossary.note: The rustle of wind.
To be held up, to stay long.
To coil around.

tangduoling.background: Wu Wenying was a Southern Song poet with the literary name Mengchuang. His style is dense and ornate, and this is one of his plainer and smoother works.

busuanzi_lu.summary: A two-part short song lyric (ci) to the tune Busuanzi. Lu You writes about the plum blossom: it blooms alone beyond the post station by a broken bridge, with no master, meeting wind and rain; it does not fight for spring or fear the envy of other flowers, and even fallen into mud its scent remains. It stands for the poet's own lofty and steadfast character.
busuanzi_lu.translation:
Beyond the post station, beside the broken bridge,
it blooms lonely, with no owner.
Already alone at dusk with its sorrow,
and then wind and rain besides.
It has no wish to struggle for spring,
and leaves the crowd of flowers to envy it.
Fallen, turned to mud and ground to dust,
only its scent remains as before.

glossary.en: yi wai - beyond the post station
glossary.note: Outside the post station, a remote place.
With no one to admire or look after it.
To meet with, to be subjected to.
To press, to grind.

busuanzi_lu.background: Lu You was a patriotic poet of the Southern Song who all his life urged resistance against the Jin and had a rough career. In this lyric he compares himself to the plum blossom, which does not follow common ways.

chaitoufeng.summary: A two-part song lyric (ci) to the tune Chaitoufeng. Lu You meets his former wife Tang Wan again at Shen Garden and looks back, sighing that the east wind is cruel and joy is thin. The vows remain but letters cannot be sent. The three 'wrong!' and the three 'let it be!' are tragic and painful.

glossary.en: hong su shou - soft red hands
glossary.note: A woman's hands, rosy and delicate.
Official wine sealed in yellow. Teng is read teng.
To live apart, away from one's group.
The silk said to be woven by mermaids; here a handkerchief.

glossary.en: xian chi ge - idle pond and pavilion
glossary.note: The pond and pavilions of Shen Garden left empty and neglected.

chaitoufeng.background: Lu You and Tang Wan were husband and wife, but were forced apart because Lu You's mother did not like her. Some years later they met by chance at Shen Garden in Shaoxing, and Lu You wrote this on the wall. Tang Wan later wrote an answering lyric and soon died of grief. The account is in Zhou Mi's Qidong yeyu, and some scholars doubt it is true.

niannujiao_zhang.summary: A two-part long song lyric (ci) to the tune Niannujiao. Zhang Xiaoxiang crosses Lake Dongting near the Mid-Autumn night: the water is clear and windless under the moon, a world of jade. He compares his pure heart to the scene, pours the Dipper slowly, makes the ten thousand things his guests, and at the end taps the boat's side and whistles alone, forgetting self and things. The vision is wide.
niannujiao_zhang.translation:
Dongting and Qingcao, near Mid-Autumn, not a breath of wind.
Thirty thousand acres of jade realm, fields of gems,
and I a single leaf of boat in the midst.
The white moon shares its light, the Milky Way joins its reflection,
inside and out all is clear.
Happy, the heart understands;
the wonder is hard to tell you.
I think of years in the Lingnan seas,
my lonely light shining on itself, my liver and gall all ice and snow.
My short hair is thin and rustling, my sleeves cold,
but I float steadily over the vast Canglang.
I scoop up the whole West River,
slowly pour out the Northern Dipper,
and make the ten thousand things my guests.
Tapping the gunwale, I whistle alone,
and do not know what night this night is.

glossary.en: Dongting Qingcao - Lake Dongting and Lake Qingcao
glossary.note: Dongting Lake and Qingcao Lake are joined.

glossary.en: yu jie qiong tian - a realm of jade, fields of gems
glossary.note: The lake under moonlight like a field of jade.

glossary.en: Ling hai jing nian - years in the south
glossary.note: Many years in Lingnan. Zhang Xiaoxiang had served as military commissioner of Guangxi.
Blue-green water; the wide river and lake.
To ladle up. Read yi.

niannujiao_zhang.background: Zhang Xiaoxiang was a Southern Song poet. In 1166 he was dismissed from office and went north, and wrote this lyric as he passed Lake Dongting. It has the open-hearted manner of Su Shi.

linjiangxian_yan.summary: A two-part song lyric (ci) to the tune Linjiangxian. When he wakes from dream and drink, Yan Jidao sits in a locked tower with curtains hanging, remembering when he first saw Little Ping and how she spoke of longing on the pipa. The bright moon is the same, but the coloured cloud has gone, and he mourns a person gone and a tower empty.

glossary.note: A singing girl in the house of a friend of Yan Jidao.

glossary.en: xin zi luo yi - a gauze dress with the heart character
glossary.note: A gauze robe embroidered with a design of the character for heart, or a robe perfumed with 'heart-character' incense.
A figure for a beautiful woman; here, Little Ping.

glossary.term: 落花人獨立，微雨燕雙飛
glossary.en: luo hua ren du li, wei yu yan shuang fei - fallen flowers, a person alone; fine rain, a pair of swallows
glossary.note: Adapted from lines by Weng Hong of the Five Dynasties.

linjiangxian_yan.background: Yan Jidao was a son of Yan Shu and a Northern Song poet. His lyrics mostly deal with the past and with singing girls, and carry deep feeling.

zhegutian_yan.summary: A two-part song lyric (ci) to the tune Zhegutian. Yan Jidao remembers the dream of meeting a singing girl again: in the old days she offered wine and sang and danced; after parting, he thought of her and dreamed of her. In the last lines, holding a silver lamp at the reunion, he still fears it is a dream. The feeling is true and deep.

glossary.en: pan que - to be ready to risk
glossary.note: To be ready to throw oneself in. Read pan.

glossary.en: wu di yang liu lou xin yue - dancing until the moon sank to the willow tops
glossary.note: The dance went on so long that the moon over the tower sank down to the tips of the willows.

glossary.en: ge jin tao hua shan di feng - singing until the wind of the peach-blossom fan died
glossary.note: They sang until the fan stopped stirring the air: a joy in song and dance.
A lamp of silver.

zhegutian_yan.background: This is one of Yan Jidao's best-known lyrics. The line 'still afraid that this meeting is only a dream' draws on the sense of Du Fu's lines, 'late in the night we light the candle again and face each other as if in a dream'.

busuanzi_li.summary: A two-part short song lyric (ci) to the tune Busuanzi. In the plain voice of a folk song, Li Zhiyi writes that the two live at the head and foot of the Yangtze and drink the same river's water, using the endless river as a picture of endless longing, and hopes their hearts are alike and will not fail their longing.
busuanzi_li.translation:
I live at the head of the Long River,
you live at the foot of the Long River;
every day I think of you and do not see you,
but we drink of the same river water.
When will this water stop?
When will this sorrow end?
I only wish your heart were like mine,
and then you will not fail my longing.

glossary.en: Chang Jiang tou, Chang Jiang wei - the head and foot of the Yangtze
glossary.note: The upper and lower reaches of the Yangtze.
To cease.
To finish.

glossary.en: ding bu fu - surely will not fail
glossary.note: Will certainly not let down.

busuanzi_li.background: Li Zhiyi was a Northern Song poet who was good at the short lyric. This poem is plain in language like a folk song, and the feeling is sincere.
